If there is no further discussion of this matter perhaps the committee would wish me to make a ruling now. This ruling is on the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition earlier this afternoon. The amendment reads as follows:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"The government give consideration to introducing a measure to amend the Old Age Security Act, effective with respect to months beginning with January, 1967, to provide for the payment out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund and for charging to the Old Age Security Fund under that Act of an additional monthly amount of $25 to all pensioners thereunder.
During the time that has elapsed since the amendment was moved the Chair has had an opportunity to give serious and careful consideration to the validity or regularity of the proposed amendment. I suggest to the committee that the Chair entertains serious doubts that this proposal is indeed an amendment. It would appear that the amendment in the first instance is in the nature of an alternative scheme, and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre during the course of his remarks stated that it is an alternative scheme. But as such it would be an expanded negative.
If the amendment were ruled to be in order and adopted by this committee the main question, which is the consideration of the resolution proposed by the minister, would be terminated. This committee of the whole, as are all committees of this house, is limited in its

deliberation to the terms of its order of reference-in this case the terms of the resolution proposed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare which was referred to the committee of the whole house.
Under the heading "Procedure in committee of the whole house on expenditure" in May's seventeenth edition, page 798, the following is stated under the subheading "Procedure on amendments":
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
The approval or the reduction of the expenditure under consideration, or an increase in the stringency of the terms and conditions of the charge thereby created, are the matters specially entrusted to such a committee, and to these objects amendments are directed.
An amendment proposing to substitute for the resolution an argumentative justification for the refusal of the demand is out of order, as are also amendments proposed with a view to substituting an alternative scheme to that proposed with the royal recommendation.
If the committee would permit the Chair to make a further reference to May's seventeenth edition at page 632, I should like to read a paragraph appearing under the heading "Reasoned amendments", which says:
Since the primary purpose of the committee is to consider and amend in detail matters which have been referred to it, and since such matters have, in the case of bills, previously been agreed to in principle by the house or, in the case of the three kinds of committees dealing with public charges . . . are matters in which the initiative properly belongs to the government, it is not usually in order in committee of the whole house to move an amendment to leave out all the words after the first word in a resolution in order to add other words. There are precedents, however, for amendments of this type being moved in committee of the whole House upon resolutions (not imposing charges) which were preliminary to the introduction of bills.
Respecting my earlier remarks having to do with the proposed amendment being in order as an alternative proposal or alternative scheme, I refer the committee to section 4 of citation 250 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which reads as follows:
The fundamental terms of a money resolution submitted to the house with the Governor-General's recommendation upon which a committee of the whole is set up cannot be amended. Amendments will only be in order if they fall within the terms of the resolution. The procedure in committee on those resolutions follows in principle the procedure of the committee of supply, and amendments are out of order if they are proposed with a view to substituting an alternative scheme to that proposed with the royal recommendation.
For all these reasons, with all deference to the right hon. Leader of the Opposition I have to rule the amendment out of order.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose
we on this side could have anticipated your decision. Nevertheless, we must make every effort possible for the senior citizens of this country, as we have done during the course of the entire session.
A comparison was made between the minister and Scrooge who is known to us from the legendary story which has been handed down to us. Scrooge might be pardoned for his attitude because he was stupid, but in this case I believe it is deceit. I believe the senior citizens of the country are being deceived.
Not too long ago, referring to myself and to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the minister said that we were adopting our attitude for the sake of publicity. Again, on November 23, in a C.B.C. program called "Preview Commentary" one Marcel Gingras said the same thing. I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the committee that every position we have taken on old age security has been vindicated and proven true as the result of the explanation given to us this afternoon. That applies equally to the statement I made about leaks of information to the Toronto Star. That statement is also true, because we had proof this afternoon that it is so. We are getting used to that in the house as a way of operation by this government. I think it is high time it was brought to an end.
The minister had little enough to say about the appeal board and the position it will have under this legislation. Again I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that what has been done is extremely retrograde when we consider how old age pensions were initially constituted in Canada. Under a Liberal administration in 1950-51 every senior citizen became entitled by right at age 70 to participate in the old age security program. The decision taken by the Liberal government in 1956 and at the beginning of 1957 was not as serious to my mind as the step the minister took in this house today.
I hope that there are backbenchers in the Liberal party who in this instance are willing to stand up and say that the government is wrong because fundamentally that is how they feel. There is no question of the truth of that. We shall see what those backbenchers do in due course.
As was pointed out by an hon. member this afternoon, in 1956-57 the government used the balance in the old age security account for its own purposes. Fifty million dollars was taken out for this and for that so that the fund would look poor and emaciated. Now the government is playing with larger sums of
Old Age Security Act Amendment money. Let me remind the committee of what the minister said during the discussion of another piece of social legislation. The minister was being questioned by the hon. member for Simcoe East about money that was to be used and he said, as reported at page 7938 of Hansard:
Frankly, I do not attach any real Importance to these figures. I do not attach any real importance to-
Then the amount of money, a large amount, is mentioned specifically. The minister was also being questioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The money involved ran to millions and millions of dollars. But those millions were not important then. Surely, bearing in mind the unanimous point made by the joint committee concerned with this matter in 1950 and 1951, the money was important then and is important today. Is the m nister bringing in a new era of political thinking? If the minister is thinking about the amount of money that will be needed by the end of the fiscal year for any increase and il he is projecting that amount into the future, 1 do not think he need be concerned. He need not be concerned about the amendment this afternoon which sought to increase the old age pension by $25. I shall show why in a moment. The minister himself several times said it would be worth while increasing the pension by $25 across the board.
One looks at the cost of administration and then one looks at the money saved by eliminating the $500 tax free for those aged 65 to 70. Income tax will be collected from people in a taxable bracket. I should like to see all the money involved detailed so that we might know how much the program would cost the government because, frankly, I do not think it would cost the government that much. The minister may not agree with me, but then the minister wants to impress his view on the committee. He has impressed his view on the cab net.

Mr. Chairman, as I considered the government's proposal in connection with old age pension legislation I was reminded of a newspaper picture I saw a short time ago in New York. It depicted a woman boycotting a supermarket. She was pushing a baby in a baby carriage. The carriage carried a sign which stated: Daddy cannot afford me because I cost too much to feed. As I listened to the minister's explanation this afternoon I felt that the elderly people of this country must feel much the same way toward the government-Daddy cannot afford me because I cost too much to feed.
I am sure the elderly people of this country have come to the conclusion this year that almost all other segments of the population have enjoyed an increased income. The crowning indignation of elderly people I am sure occurred as a result of reports a few days ago to the effect that within two hours this house approved one and a half billion dollars for expenditures of various kinds. When we consider the amount of money this house has approved in the past few days it is no wonder that elderly constituents, like one who resides in my constituency, have written and said: This government has barrels of money but none for us.
The minister this afternoon wove a very capable web of words, but behind that web of words could be observed a veritable jungle of administrative difficulties and red tape. This jungle has been created to persuade the elderly people of this country that there is a great deal more in this legislation for them than there actually is. My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, very quickly cut through the jungle of red tape and confusion and brought to light the difficulties that will ensue as a result of the shortcomings of this legislation.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
There is no need for me to emphasize the facts which he brought out, but I do feel sure that elderly people went through a lot of difficulty, that they needed help and guidance and that they turned to many people in order even to establish their birth dates at the time the old age security pension legislation was first introduced. I cannot help but believe that they will be in very difficult straits indeed if they have to go through all this bureaucracy in connection with the amendment now before us.
This evening I wish to make two points to underline what I think is basically wrong
10736	COMMONS
Old Age Security Act Amendment with the legislation. I will deal with them as simply and plainly as I possibly can. First, I believe that this legislation undermines the whole principle of the old age security pension legislation. Second, I believe that the proposed amount is completely unrelated to the needs of elderly people. In connection with my first point let me say that the old age security pension legislation established a most important right, namely, the right of any person who has reached a certain age to receive an old age pension with no questions asked. This did not come easily.
In 1927 the first old age pension was $20 a month at the age of 70 with a means test. Step by step through the 1930's and 1940's the amount was raised until in 1951, as has been so eloquently expressed by a number of hon. members, the Old Age Security Act emerged, not as the brainchild of one party in this house but as the considered opinion of a committee representing all parties in the house, the members of which in turn represented the elderly people from wide sections of this country. The 1951 Old Age Security Act gave $40 a month at the age of 70 with no means test. In effect it wiped out the necessity of a means test. Then, election by election through the 1950's and 1960's the amount was raised until in 1963 the present amount of $75 a month was reached.
Since 1963 there has been no change in the $75 pension. The amount is still the same in spite of the fact that since 1963 there has been an over-all rise in the cost of living of around 10 per cent. Food, rent and health care are the three factors which bear most heavily on the old people of this country. These three factors taken together have risen by as much as a third in the cost of living since 1963. Indeed, it would probably take the whole $105 or very close to it to bring the old age pension up to the purchasing power of the $75 at the time that amount was first established.
This legislation will turn the calendar back 15 years. It will bring back the hated means test. To call it a needs test will not make the means test any sweeter to the old people of this country. The minister says there will be no welfare people prowling around and nosing into the affairs of the pensioners. That is true, but the old people themselves will be expected to police their own affairs and this will not improve matters.

Mr. Chairman, with far less fire, vigour and enthusiasm, but I hope with a bit more logic, I should like to deal with some of the points raised with regard to the resolution before us to provide an income supplement for certain pensioners. This is a supplement to be provided those who have no steady or significant source of income other than the basic old age pension itself, though there are certain other exceptions in the form of social assistance, disability pensions and the like.
To me, the key word in this resolution is "supplement". I think no one denies the entitlement of all our senior citizens to a basic old age pension as a matter of right, and there is nothing in this resolution to contradict this principle. However, an argument against any supplement for people who are in need in my opinion lacks, in the first place, moral realism.

It obviously follows that in order to supplement the basic universal payment to those who require more there simply must be the establishment of some criterion by which to judge that requirement. Those who stubbornly refuse to see any other way to handle this situation but to increase the basic pension constantly seem to me to overlook the fact that whatever the basic amount for practical purposes it could never be enough to meet the needs of some people who have no other source of sustenance. Continually to look after these people with a flat rate increase to all is continually to hand out public money to many who simply do not need it. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it appears to me that there must always be some method by which those less fortunate may receive further help from the public purse. In other words, there must be devised a method to provide additional help to those in additional need.
Because of the need to be selective there must be a standard of qualification for this extra assistance. As one newspaper editorial recently put it, it seems to me that there is much more rhetoric than reason in the attack on this plan by the opposition parties. The bogey of the degradation of a means test and the argument that the qualifying yardstick robs the aged of their dignity is pure nonsense. The proposed measure of eligibility is clearly one of income declaration, the release of which information Canadians have been used to for years and years. Certainly most Canadians feel no injury to their dignity when they fill out their income tax forms, and as far as I can tell they certainly take no offence on those happy but rather rare occasions when they receive an income tax rebate cheque.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Surely this measure guaranteeing incomes must be recognized as one of the most simple, impersonal and fair measures to be introduced and suggested in contemporary times. Most certainly the measure bears no resemblance to the old type of means test in existence during depression days. Undoubtedly that was humiliating and degrading and very few Canadians would countenance a return of that type of bureaucratic imposition. To attempt to describe this legislation as employing the same test I suggest is trying to make political capital, is distorting the truth and is irresponsible.
I should like in passing to comment on some of the merits of this legislation as I see them. All or nearly all senior Canadians will share in the Canada Pension Plan. We had to recognize, however, that there was a gap between

the present and the time when that program would take full effect, and the proposed income supplement program will certainly fill the void without becoming a permanent drain on the old age pension fund. These three pieces of major legislation are needed to complete our social welfare program.

I think we should be very proud when we compare the standard of our pension plan for the aged with the pension plans of all the enlightened countries of the world. Speaking a few moments ago the hon. member gave some interesting facts on this topic. Reference was made to the high level attained by the Swedish pension plan. It must be remembered, Mr. Chairman, that that level is reached through a contributory plan similar to the one introduced by this government in the Canada Pension Plan. The effect of that will be felt in a very few years.
I should not like to close my remarks without taking the opportunity to thank and congratulate Senator Croll and his colleagues of the special committee of the Senate on aging which studied the problems of our senior citizens with such compassion and wisdom. This enlightened legislation to some degree is, I think, their brainchild. We are recognizing in law for the first time so far as I know the principle of a guaranteed income. This is a break-through, and I shall support the bill wholeheartedly.

Mr. Chairman, we welcome one feature of this bill, the recognition that our old people cannot possibly live on $75 a month. When it comes to the final vote no doubt some members will be constrained to vote for this bill because of that single fact. But I for one think that a means test for our old people is absolutely wrong. It is wrong not only because it will bring out inaccurate figures; it is wrong because $100 a month or $105 a month is not enough to live on.
A member on the government side said we were either stupid, perverse or both if we could not see the difference between a guaranteed income and a means test. I will not take up the time of the committee arguing that point. I say that one is stupid if one does not know that a person today, especially a person living in a city, needs a guaranteed income well above $100 a month. It is indeed necessary to see the difference between a guaranteed income and what this program is.
Surely no one is contending that this bill gives everybody in Canada a basic living. We have not got to the point yet, it seems, of thinking that the old age pension is intended to provide a complete living for our old people. But I contend, Mr. Chairman, that $105 a month is so much below the necessary income level for any person in Canada, married or single, that it is only a question of how much we can afford to pay these people. How much can the gross national product provide for these people? We ought to take a sober look at our country to see what social security we can afford. I think we should be able to afford a basic living to every man, woman and child in Canada but on the basis that we as Canadians should all be willing to work for that basic security.
I stand here as a Conservative and say that we ought to pay, at this present stage in our history, a guaranteed income to give security to our old people because they have not had the opportunity in the past, as the hon. member for Simcoe East said, to earn and save money. They have not had the ability to do it. Certainly, with inflation galloping at the rate it has, our old people have not had the opportunity of putting away money after paying for rent, food and drugs.
Taking the figure of $105 a month you do not have to be very bright, once you start working our what you need, to come to the conclusion that perhaps $150 a month might have been closer to the basic minimum. So I
December 5, 196&

Old Age Security Act Amendment entirely reject the argument about a guaranteed income because if this pension plan purports to provide a guaranteed income to enable our people to live in health, reasonable comfort and security, $105 is a pitiful sum of money.
I do not know whether the Minister of Finance can find enough money to pay for this program. I know that in recent months a certain amount of magic has come from his department. They found close to $55 million, some say $110 million, just like that. I suggest that if we need $500 million the minister ought to look in the crystal ball or take Aladdin's lamp and rub it and get this sum. If we have not enough money to pay to our old people to enable them to live in comfort, then we had better go back to work. We had better smarten up our whole economy so that it can produce the money.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
We have been told about the pension plan in Sweden. What type of excuse is it to point to Sweden, a country with limited resources, and say that they give their people a certain basic standard of living and it will be good enough if we do the same here. I do not agree. Canada, so far as the proportion of natural resources to population is concerned, is the richest country in the world and if there is any problem about giving our old folks a reasonable standard of comfort we need to look hard at our own ability to work and at the courage of our governments at all levels to stop giving money to the bums and make sure that they give it to the old people who have worked already and who have earned our undying gratitude.
I suggest we stop wasting money by the hundreds of millions on building islands in a river, putting on expensive television programs and sending members of the press on wild excursions to Europe to dig out filth, and that we should spend some of that money looking after our old people. I would have respect for a budget which said that we had to tighten our belts. But I do not think we have to tighten our belts at all. I think we have to roll up our sleeves.
It is time we got back to the dynamic program of the previous administration when we decided that the way to pay our bills and support our old people was to sell our products in the markets of the world, to develop the brains of our young people by technical training, to build new railroads into the wilderness instead of abandoning railroads, to dam the rivers we have and stop the pollution


of our streams instead of whining about being short of water. If we want to find money for our old people, stop wasting it on those who are abusing the unemployment insurance fund. I am not looking for votes from people like that. I would say that any young man or woman capable of working in Canada today should be given an opportunity to work and that no welfare or relief of any kind should be provided in affluent times such as these. I do not speak with any golden spoon in my mouth. There has never been a golden spoon in my mouth. During the great depression which my hon. friend from Simcoe East spoke about tonight I worked every day for very small wages. If I was of retiring age today, it would not be any money I earned between 1930 and 1950 which could have been put into a fund of any kind.
All I ask of our young people today is that they do what our grandfathers did and what our mothers and fathers did. They took up the challenge of a country which was a wilderness and they built it up until we have now what is, I suppose, the second highest standard of living in the world. That was not done by socialism and it was not done by wishful thinking. It was done by hard work and thrift, and as a Conservative I do not know any substitute which is a satisfactory answer to Canada's needs. I know that the people of Canada are willing to work and I know that those of us who have worked and who are able and willing to pay taxes do not want any penny-pinching budgetary arguments which would deny to our fathers and mothers and to our grandfathers and grandmothers the right to partake in this rich feast which they at least have so rightly deserved.
I do not like double-talk. We have the money if we want to find it. We owe this debt to our old people. Those who want to pay it do not call such an action socialism. It is a debt. It is a debt of honour, more so because these people have actually done the work. We should only be paying them the wages they have already earned.
I think the money can be found and again I say that if our monetary experts say the money cannot be found we had better find ways and means of creating new wealth with the sweat of our brows so that we can follow one of the oldest standards in our Judo-Christian civilization, that of giving to our older people, our fathers and our mothers, the honour which is due to them. I know no better way of honouring our fathers and our mothers than by paying them the money which they have so richly deserved.

Mr. Chairman, I should first of all like to indicate that I support any measure which will improve the circumstances of the old age pensioners of this nation and help them to maintain themselves more easily as free citizens. However, unlike hon. members on the other side, I believe this could best be done by continuing to adopt the principle laid down in the Old Age Security Act which made old age security a pensionable right of every citizen who paid income tax in this nation. By the resolution we are considering today we are asked to indicate our belief in a new thesis so far as older citizens and old age security are concerned. In other words, we are moving into the field of welfare rather than remaining in the field of old age security. We are indicating that we believe in a means test or, as the minister puts it, a needs test.
It amazes me that the minister should say: do not get the idea that by this proposal we intend to investigate people; we shall ask them to tell us what their income is and on that basis we shall inform them whether they qualify for the increased pension and also whether they qualify for assistance. If we adopt the approach recommended by the government it will be necessary first of all to increase the number of civil servants in order to provide the investigators who will be required to check the reports made by applicants. Those reports must then be examined to determine whether or not the applicants are telling the truth. In other words, we would have to carry out the same procedures as are now followed in connection with old age assistance. I do not know what additional cost to the treasury this would involve. I do know that in my area of Canada the officials who carry out this work at the present time are overburdened. There is no indication that there will be a lessening of their work if we include, as I believe the minister indicated, an additional 900,000 people. If we are to take this approach then we are basically putting into effect the same scheme as when the old age assistance program was introduced, and I do not think this is good enough. I do not think this is what the people want.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Surely the taxpayers should be telling us, their representatives, what in effect they are willing to pay for. I think the taxpayers of this nation are willing to pay for an increase in old age security with no strings attached to it. During the last election campaign, when I spoke with people, whether young or old, and

Old Age Security Act Amendment discussed this subject with them, they indicated strong approval of the $25 per month increase that we proposed in our program.
I do not think that making the increase effective as of January 1, 1967, is fair or equitable in view of the fact that the government has contributed to the cost of living spiral which in a most detrimental way has affected the livelihood of the people we are talking about. No old age pensioner can say he is as well off today as he was on January 1, 1966 and this by a long shot. The government has been a party to agreements that have had a significant effect on the cost of living. It has agreed to very substantial increases in the salaries of many Canadians. Yet it now says to the old age pensioner, You must wait until January 1, 1967, before you get anything and then the amount you will get will depend on the kind of income report you make.
I deplore this kind of approach. It shows no real feeling for the problems of people who find themselves in difficult straits. During the recent medicare debate we saw a government that is willing to sacrifice principle to the dollar. During the election campaign it promised the people certain things but immediately the election was over it started watering down its promises because of financial considerations.
In some fields this approach may be all right. We may say that problems which need solution must wait because of the financial difficulties in which we find ourselves. But this is not the case so far as old age security recipients are concerned. They are the people who are deserving of every possible consideration from whatever government is in office.
What about other people? What about the people who are being asked to contribute certain amounts from their income tax every year for old age security purposes? We are saying to them, There is one level of old age security for you and there is another level for someone else. In doing this we are moving away from the basic concept that every Canadian who pays income tax is making a contribution to a pension which he will receive as a right when he reaches a certain age. That should be the only basis for qualifying.
There is nothing which frightens me more than the proliferation of jobs in the civil service. This plan in effect removes to a certain degree the freedom of the individual to enjoy certain rights without investigation. We are now moving into one more area in which we will add another group of troops to the civil

Old Age Security Act Amendment service and thereby eliminate that much more freedom of the individual. If we are to be realistic we must produce the kind of legislation that will put all Canadians in the same position. We are not doing that with this resolution and the bill that will follow it.
We will not be keeping faith with our older people, the people who have made their contribution to the building of Canada, the people who went through the great depression from 1930 onward, who found themselves in a position where they could not save money, unlike people who are working today, but had to fight the good fight sometimes with less than a subsistence income. Let us be realistic. There is no one in this chamber who would want to try to subsist on $105 a month. Yet we are saying to anyone in this position, sure, you can have an increase and you probably need it to remain healthy and alive, if that is possible on $105 a month, but you are going to have to submit yourself to certain degrading tests which will show that you may be able to have only half of the $30 that is available, because of this, that or the other thing. I do not think that is good enough. I think we should be bigger than that.
We members of parliament sit here in this chamber and in committees and talk about food prices and how they have increased. Yet as members of parliament we are debating today the rules and regulations under which we will give these people $30. Are we not really being big people when we say to them that in order to get this they must do this, that and the other thing.

We are told by the Minister of Finance that if the old age security payment is to be increased in any way there must be an increase

in taxes. On what basis are the people going to be taxed? Is he going to add an additional percentage point to the old age security program? Surely if we are to be asked to pay an increased amount of tax the Minister of Finance should be asked to give us some indication of how he expects these additional revenues to be raised and who will be contributing to them. I think it would have been a much simpler procedure and would have been much more readily acceptable to everyone in Canada if the minister had been willing to increase old age security payments by the use of the same formula which has been in existence. With the increasing cost of living, with the many additional obligations faced by the older people today, along with the fact that people are living to an older age because of the improved health facilities in our nation, although at the same time they are dependent during their longer life on advanced medical science and the medicines which are available, one would think that he would see to it that these people are able to maintain themselves without having the necessity to become involved in a means or needs test. In other words, they should not have to find themselves in the position where they have to submit themselves to investigation.
I support anything which will be of assistance to the older citizens of our nation. I support this program, if no other program is available, because anything which will assist these people is of benefit to them and they need the assistance. I believe, however, that as members of this house we could find a much more forthright approach to a solution of their problems than is indicated by this legislation. I believe we should be as straightforward with them as we are with the university students. If we were willing to go over the financial commitments of the government I believe we would find many areas in which we might reduce the amount of assistance now being made available. I think the C.B.C. is an outstanding example. Perhaps we would then find that we would be able to make the money available so that these Canadian citizens would not have to face an investigation

and meet requirements which are not in keeping with the dignity which we would like them to have. We think nothing of giving $100 million to the C.B.C. to operate every year. Old Age Security Amendment
I do not wish to dwell any longer on this particular point. Tonight, after a year in office, the government has brought down its program, its policy for the older people of this country which provides them with a minimum income. Had this minimum income been paid across the board to all old age pensioners in addition to the old age security pension I would have been a happy man tonight because then the position I have taken all along Would have been proved right. I would have represented Liberal party thought in this country although perhaps a little in advance.
I still believe that the legislation which the government has proposed today is not the best. I feel that the Canadian Welfare Council agrees with me and that all major welfare organizations also agree with me. They are in favour of a minimum income but they are in favour of it being paid to everyone regardless of the income of the recipient. If their incomes were high under such an arrangement taxpayers might have it taxed away, but they would at least receive it.
I should like to commend the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace for his speech. He stated that there was no means test in the proposed legislation. In my view there is a means test. The applicant for the supplement to the old age pension must show that his or her income falls below the minimum or else he or she cannot qualify for it. The proposed legislation forces people to prove they are poverty-stricken before they can qualify for the supplement. In my view, and I admit it to be only an individual view but I give it as a member of parliament, this is scarcely the Canadian thing to do at this time. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we have a means test in front of us.

I have a man working for me as a gardener. He is an old age pensioner and I like him very much. But I support it in general because I am forced tor in fearing that if I oppose it I will in reality be opposing a step forward toward a truly minimum retirement income that may come some day for all Canadians.
It was pointed out to me tonight a few moments ago by an hon. member of this house that if this supplement were paid to everyone the whole basis of the Canada Pension Plan would have to be changed or it would be thrown out of gear. I believe this may be correct, and for that reason a minimum income to everyone might have to be adjusted when the Canada Pension Plan starts paying money to recipients. Therefore I am going to reserve the balance of my remarks until a later date.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this stage of the debate obviously I will make my remarks brief. The last hon. member who addressed the committee pointed out something that members on both sides already know, that no matter what semantics the minister employs his legislation involves a retrograde step. Call it a needs test or any other test you like, the minister in his haste to put legislation on the statute books that will do him credit is in fact reverting to a means test. The hon. member who has just spoken has made the record abundantly clear. No amount of semantics on the minister's part will change the record. This is a test. The hon. member who has just taken his seat pointed out that this measure will definitely impinge upon people over 70 who want to lead an active life and receive certain remuneration for their efforts. In brief, Mr. Chairman, this legislation is ill-considered, hasty and involves a means test, be it called anything else by the minister and the government who are trying to hasten its passage through parliament.
The main reason for my rising tonight is simply to say in the closing minutes of the debate that many Canadians are frankly worried about the future of this country vis-a-vis federal-provincial relations and constitutional reform. I am not saying for one minute that
December 5, 1966

we should always be paying attention to Quebec to the exclusion of the rest of Canada. But I did ask the Prime Minister today a succinct question in these terms: In view of the throne speech emanating from the Quebec legislature last week, in view of what the government of Quebec has said about the necessity of constitutional reform, and in view of what all the other provinces have been saying to this government about the need for constitutional reform over the last months, has the time not now come for the government to decide on definite action in order that this nation in its centennial year may obtain a made in Canada constitution suited to modern times?
Why does the government without consulting the provinces in a conjoined area of jurisdiction under the constitution now rush into this issue pretending that nothing is wrong? Cannot the government read the writing on the wall and realize that once again by acting unilaterally in a field such as pensions they are only exacerbating the situation? Does the government not realize, having read the throne speech which was issued from Quebec and having listened, if they ever do listen, to the other provincial premiers, that the time has now come for basic constitutional reform?
What this country needs today is a modern constitution which is made in Canada and is suited to modern times. I proclaim to this committee tonight that the minister is rushing headlong into difficulties not only with Quebec but with the other provinces. Pretending that the provinces do not exist, that there never was a throne speech in Quebec last week, that Mr. Johnson has said nothing about pensions, that there has been no such thing as a federal-provincial meeting during the last few weeks and that the present constitution is perfectly satisfactory, the government is unilaterally plunging into a conjoined area, namely, that of constitutional reform.
